meta.blurb: Go and watch an ant, says one old saying, and learn how to work. The Book of Proverbs holds ancient Israel's short, sharp advice on money, friends, words and temper, and a wisdom that calls out loudly in the market square.
meta.bible: Proverbs: a book of the Hebrew Bible, also part of the Christian Old Testament, made of short sayings and longer poems about wisdom. Solomon: the king of ancient Israel, famous for his wisdom, to whom tradition credits many of the sayings. Israel: the ancient kingdom and people where the book began. Wisdom: pictured in the book as a woman who calls out to everyone. Folly: Wisdom's opposite, also pictured as a woman. The Lord: the name the book uses for God. Hezekiah: a king of Judah whose men, the book says, copied out more of Solomon's proverbs. Agur: the writer of the thirtieth chapter. Bible. Hebrew. Judah. Chapters one to nine: a father speaking to his son. Chapters ten to twenty-two: short two-line sayings. The Sayings of the Wise: a section that begins in chapter twenty-two. Chapter thirty-one: the poem of the capable woman. Voice and tone: calm, warm, practical and respectful. Every saying is attributed to the book. The words are the book's own ideas retold, never long quotations. Where a saying can be understood in more than one way, say so. Never preach or compare faiths.

B1B2: The Book of Proverbs is a collection of short, wise sayings from ancient Israel. Tradition says that most of them come from King Solomon, although the book grew over time and had several authors.
The book says that respect for the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. Here the word fear is usually understood as deep respect and awe, and fools, the book says, despise wisdom and instruction.
A father tells his son to listen to his instruction and never to forget his mother's teaching. Their advice, he says, will be like a beautiful crown on his head and a chain of gold around his neck.

Some people will say to the young man, come with us, and we will take whatever we want from others. Do not go with them, says the father, because the traps that they set for others will in the end catch them.

In a famous passage, Wisdom is pictured as a woman who calls out in the streets and the markets. She asks how long the simple will love being simple, and she promises to share her thoughts with all who listen.

If you search for wisdom as you would search for silver, says the writer, you will understand what it means to respect God. Wisdom is a gift from the Lord, he says, but it comes to those who are willing to look for it.
Trust in the Lord with all your heart, says the writer, and do not lean on your own understanding. If you remember him in everything you do, he will make your paths straight.
The writer tells his readers to honour the Lord with their wealth and with the first part of their harvest. Then, he says, their barns will be full and their vats will overflow with new wine.
Happy is the person who finds wisdom, says the writer, because she is worth more than silver and gold. Her ways are pleasant, and all her paths lead to peace.

Do not hold back help from someone who needs it, says the writer, if you are able to give it. Do not say, come back tomorrow, when you can help today, and never plan harm against a neighbour who trusts you.
The writer remembers his own father teaching him when he was young and tender. Get wisdom, his father said, and whatever else you get, get understanding.

The path of the righteous is like the first light of dawn, says the writer, and it shines brighter and brighter until the full day. The way of the wicked, however, is like deep darkness, and they do not know what makes them fall.
Above everything else, says the writer, guard your heart, because the whole course of your life flows from it. In the Bible the heart means the centre of a person's thoughts, wishes and choices.
Let your eyes look straight ahead, says the writer, and think carefully about the path for your feet. Do not turn to the right or to the left, but keep your feet away from evil.

In these chapters the father warns his son against being led away from faithfulness in marriage. He uses the picture of water and says, drink from your own well, and be happy with the wife of your youth.
Go and look at the ant, you lazy person, says the writer, and learn from its ways. It has no ruler to command it, yet it stores up food in summer and gathers its harvest in good time.

The writer says that there are six things the Lord hates, and a seventh that he cannot stand. They include proud eyes, a lying tongue, a heart that plans evil, and a person who stirs up quarrels among brothers.
In chapter eight, Wisdom speaks about herself, and she says that she was with God before the hills and the seas were made. She was beside him, she says, and she was full of delight every day.
Wisdom builds her house and prepares a feast, and she invites everyone to come in and eat. Folly, however, is loud and knows nothing, and she calls to the same people from her own doorway.
Do not correct a mocker, says the writer, or he will hate you, but correct a wise man and he will love you. Teach a good person, and he will become wiser still.

From chapter ten, the book becomes a long list of short, two-line sayings that tradition links with Solomon. The first says that a wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son brings grief to his mother.
The book says that treasure gained by cheating does no good, but that honest living will save a person. Lazy hands bring poverty, it says, while hard-working hands bring wealth.
Hatred stirs up trouble, says the book, but love covers over every wrong. A friend who forgives does not keep a list of old mistakes.
When there are many words, says the book, wrongdoing is never far away. The wise person, however, knows when to keep his mouth closed.
The Lord hates dishonest scales, says the book, but he is pleased with a fair weight. In a market where buyers cannot check every measure, honesty matters most of all.
When pride comes, says the book, shame follows close behind, but wisdom is found with people who are humble. A person who thinks too much of himself is rarely ready to learn.
One person gives freely and still grows richer, says the book, while another holds back too much and grows poorer. Whoever refreshes other people will himself be refreshed in turn.
Where there is no guidance, says the book, a nation falls, but there is safety in having many advisers. A wise person never thinks that he has nothing to learn from others.
A person who works his land will have plenty of food, says the book, but one who chases empty dreams has no sense. The lazy person wants much and gets nothing, while the hard worker is rewarded.
Truthful lips last for ever, says the book, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment. The Lord hates lying lips, but he is pleased with people who tell the truth.
Hope that is put off makes the heart sick, says the book, but a wish that comes true is like a tree of life. The proverb shows that waiting is hard and that fulfilled hopes bring great joy.
Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, says the book, but a companion of fools suffers harm. The friends we choose, it suggests, slowly shape who we become.
A gentle answer turns away anger, says the book, but a harsh word stirs it up. Anyone who has calmed an argument with a soft reply knows that this is true.
A cheerful heart is good medicine, says the book, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones. This is a poetic saying about mood and wellbeing, and not a medical claim.
Pride goes before destruction, says the book, and a proud spirit goes before a fall. It is better, it adds, to be humble among the poor than to share riches with the proud.
A person may make many plans in his heart, says the book, but the answer finally comes from the Lord. Commit your work to the Lord, it says, and your plans will be firmly set.
Better a little with goodness, says the book, than great wealth with injustice. A dry crust eaten in peace is better than a house full of feasting and quarrels.
A friend loves at all times, says the book, and a brother is born for times of trouble. There are friends who only bring ruin, however, while others stay closer than a brother.
To answer before you have listened, says the book, is foolish and shameful. Much trouble in the world might be avoided if people first heard the whole story.
The tongue has the power of life and death, says the book, and those who love to talk will eat its fruit. What we say, it teaches, matters as much as what we do.
Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, says the book, and he will repay him for what he has done. To mock the poor, it says, is to insult the one who made them.
Many plans are in a person's mind, says the book, but it is the Lord's purpose that will stand. This saying encourages people to plan wisely and to stay humble.
A good name is better to choose than great riches, says the book, and being respected is better than silver or gold. Money can be earned again, but a reputation is hard to rebuild.

Train up a child in the way he should go, says the book, and even when he is old he will not turn from it. Parents have found hope in this saying, though it describes a general pattern and not a promise for every child.
Do not wear yourself out to get rich, says the book, and have the wisdom to stop. Riches can vanish in a moment, as if they had grown wings and flown away like an eagle.
If your enemy is hungry, says the book, give him bread, and if he is thirsty, give him water. This part of the book, according to its own words, was copied out by the men of King Hezekiah.

Do not answer a fool according to his folly, says one verse, or you will be just like him. The next verse says to answer a fool as his folly deserves, so a wise person must judge which advice fits the moment.
As iron sharpens iron, says the book, so one person sharpens another. The wounds of a friend can be trusted, it adds, but the kisses of an enemy are many.

In chapter thirty, a man named Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches, only for the food that he needs. He also says that four things are too wonderful for him, including an eagle in the sky and a snake on a rock.
The book ends with a poem about a capable woman who works hard, plans well, helps the poor and speaks with kindness. Her children rise up and call her happy, and her husband praises her.
C1C2: The Book of Proverbs, which belongs to the Hebrew Bible, is a collection of short sayings that were passed down in ancient Israel to teach people how to live well. Tradition connects many of them with King Solomon, famous for his wisdom, although scholars believe that the collection grew over many generations and includes the work of several writers. Its stated purpose, in the opening lines, is to give wisdom and instruction, and to help even the simple and the young to understand.

The famous principle at the heart of the book is that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, a line that returns again and again in its pages. Here fear is usually understood as reverence and awe before God, and not as terror, and it is the soil in which every other kind of wisdom is said to grow. Fools, by contrast, are described as those who despise wisdom and instruction, and the rest of the book can be read as a long invitation not to be one of them.

The writer, speaking in the voice of a father, urges his son to listen to the instruction of his father and not to abandon the teaching of his mother. Such guidance, he promises, will be a graceful garland on the young man's head and a chain of gold around his neck. It is a gentle opening to the long address that fills the first nine chapters, in which the older generation hands its experience to the younger.

The father warns his son that bad company will try to lead him astray, with sinners saying, come with us, let us lie in wait and take whatever we like. Do not walk in their way, he says, because the plans of such people return upon their own heads, and those who set a trap are in the end caught in it themselves. Greed, the passage concludes, destroys the very people who give way to it, however clever their schemes may seem.

Wisdom is pictured as a woman who stands in the busiest places, in the streets and at the city gates, and calls aloud to everyone who passes. She asks how long the simple will love their simplicity, and she warns that those who ignore her will one day call out when it is too late. But whoever listens to her, she says, will live in safety and will be at ease, without any dread of disaster.

If you search for wisdom as you would search for silver, the writer says, and look for it as you would for hidden treasure, then you will understand what it means to respect God. The picture is of a miner who digs patiently in hard ground, knowing that the reward is worth the labour. Wisdom, in other words, is treated as a gift that comes from God, but one that is given to those who are willing to look for it.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart, says the writer, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight, which is among the most quoted promises in the whole book. It is an invitation to humility, since it asks a person to admit that his own sight is limited and that he does not always see where the road will turn.

The writer tells his readers to honour the Lord with their wealth and with the first and best of their harvest. Then, he says, their barns will be filled with plenty and their vats will overflow with new wine, a vivid way of describing blessing in an age of farming. Most readers understand such promises as pictures of the general pattern of a good life, since other parts of the book admit that the righteous sometimes suffer.

Happy is the person who finds wisdom, says the writer, for she is worth more than silver and her profit is better than fine gold. She is more precious than rubies, and nothing that a person could wish for can be compared with her. Her ways are ways of pleasantness, he says, and all her paths lead to peace, and she is a tree of life to those who take hold of her.

Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, says the writer, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbour, come back tomorrow and I will give it to you, when you have it with you now. Nor should you plan harm against a neighbour who lives beside you in trust, for a friendship betrayed is a hard thing to mend.

The father recalls how he himself had once been a son, taught by his own father, and he passes on the lesson in its simplest form. Get wisdom, his father had told him, and whatever else you get, get understanding, and do not forget the words of my mouth. Prize her highly, and she will lift you up, and she will bring you honour when you embrace her.

The path of the righteous, the writer says, is like the first light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until the full light of day. The way of the wicked, in contrast, is like deep darkness, and they do not even know what it is that makes them stumble. The image carries a comforting message, for it suggests that a good life, though it may begin faintly, grows clearer with every step.

Above all else, guard your heart, says the writer, for everything you do flows from it. In the Bible the heart is not only the seat of feeling but the centre of a person's thoughts, wishes and choices, which is why it is thought worth such careful watching. Like a spring from which a river runs, it is the source from which the whole course of a life is shaped.

Let your eyes look directly ahead, says the father, and let your gaze be straight before you, and think carefully about the path for your feet. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left, but keep your foot from evil, so that all your ways may be firm. The advice is that of a traveller who knows how easily a person drifts from a good road without noticing it.

In the chapters that follow, the father warns his son against being drawn away from faithfulness, and he uses the picture of water to describe the joy of loyalty in marriage. Drink water from your own cistern, he says, and let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth. Faithfulness, in this view, is not a prison but a quiet source of lasting happiness.

Go to the ant, you lazy person, says the writer, consider her ways and be wise. She has no commander, no overseer and no ruler, and yet she stores her food in summer and gathers her supplies at harvest. How long, he asks the sleeper, will you lie there, for a little sleep and a little folding of the hands will bring poverty upon you like a thief.

The writer offers a list of things that the Lord hates, introducing it with the formula that six things are hated and a seventh is detestable to him. They are haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that plans wicked schemes, feet that hurry to do evil, a false witness, and one who stirs up quarrels among brothers. The list is a small portrait of how pride, deceit and violence poison a community.

In the eighth chapter, Wisdom speaks about herself and says that she was with God from the very beginning, before the hills were settled and before the seas were set in their place. In the Hebrew, her role beside him can be read as that of a skilled craftsman or as that of a delighted child, and translators have chosen both. Either way, she is said to have rejoiced in his presence every day, and to have delighted in the human race.

Wisdom is shown building her house and preparing a banquet, and she sends out her servants to invite the simple to come and eat. Folly, by contrast, is loud and restless and knows nothing, and she sits at the door of her own house calling to the very same passers-by. The two invitations stand side by side at the end of the first part of the book, and every reader must choose which door to enter.

Do not correct a mocker, says the writer, or he will hate you, but correct a wise man and he will love you. Give instruction to a wise person and he will grow wiser still, and teach a righteous person and he will add to his learning. The test of wisdom, it seems, is not whether we are ever wrong but how we respond when someone shows us that we are.

With the tenth chapter, the book changes its manner, and the long speeches of a father give way to a collection of short, two-line sayings that tradition connects with Solomon. The first of them declares that a wise son makes his father glad, but that a foolish son is a grief to his mother. Each saying stands alone, and readers have always been free to open the book at any page and take away a single thought.

Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit anyone, says the book, but righteousness delivers a person from death. The Lord does not let the righteous go hungry, it adds, though he does push aside the desire of the wicked. Lazy hands bring poverty, while diligent hands bring wealth, and the book often pairs honesty with hard work in this way.

Hatred stirs up conflict and quarrelling, says the writer, but love covers over all wrongs and keeps a household at peace. The saying does not claim that love ignores a wrong or pretends that it never happened, but that it chooses to forgive rather than to keep a record. A friend who holds on to every old injury, the proverb suggests, makes peace impossible.

When words are many, says the book, transgression is not far away, but whoever restrains his lips is wise. A great deal of trouble, from the smallest quarrel to the largest misunderstanding, begins with a sentence that should have been left unsaid. The wise person, then, learns that silence is sometimes the most intelligent answer of all.

The Lord hates dishonest scales, says the proverb, but a just weight pleases him. In the ancient marketplace, where buyers could not easily check each measure of grain or silver, a merchant's honesty was the only protection that an ordinary customer had. The saying shows that the book's wisdom is not abstract, since it deals with the practical business of buying and selling.

When pride comes, says the writer, then comes disgrace, but wisdom is found with the humble. A person who thinks too highly of himself is rarely ready to learn, and he is often the last to see his own mistakes. Humility, in this teaching, is not self-contempt but a clear and honest view of oneself.

One person gives freely and yet grows all the richer, the writer observes, while another withholds what he should give and only suffers want. A generous person will prosper, he adds, and whoever refreshes others will himself be refreshed in turn. The saying does not promise that giving brings a reward in money, but it holds that a generous life is rarely an empty one.

Where there is no guidance, says the book, a nation falls, but in an abundance of advisers there is safety. No ruler, however clever, sees everything, and a wise leader gathers different voices around him before he decides. The same holds for any person, since the humble habit of asking for advice has saved many from avoidable mistakes.

The one who works his land will have plenty of bread, says the proverb, but whoever chases empty dreams has no sense. The lazy person craves much and gets nothing, whereas the diligent are richly supplied. Time and again the book returns to the plain truth that steady, patient labour is the surest path to a secure life.

Truthful lips endure for ever, the book declares, but a lying tongue lasts only for a moment. The Lord detests lying lips, it says, and delights in those who act faithfully. The point is that a lie may serve a purpose for a day, but only the truth can be relied upon for a lifetime.

Hope deferred makes the heart sick, says the proverb, but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life. Anyone who has waited long for good news will recognise the truth of the first line, and anyone who has finally received it will understand the second. The saying holds together the pain of waiting and the joy of arrival in only a few words.

Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, says the writer, but a companion of fools suffers harm. The saying suggests that character is shaped slowly by the company that we keep, much as a traveller's clothes take on the smell of the road. The friends we choose, in other words, are among the most important teachers that we will ever have.

A gentle answer turns away wrath, says the writer, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Anyone who has calmed an argument with a soft reply knows how true this is, and anyone who has made one worse with a sharp retort knows it too. The proverb teaches that the tone of a reply can be more powerful than its content.

A cheerful heart is good medicine, says the book, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones. This is a poetic observation about the way that mood and wellbeing are connected, and not a medical claim of any kind. It suggests that joy, humour and good company are not luxuries but part of what keeps a person strong.

Pride goes before destruction, says the book, and a haughty spirit before a fall. It is better, the writer adds, to be humble in spirit among the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud. The sayings are a warning that those who think themselves too great to fail are often the ones who fall furthest.

The plans of the heart belong to a person, says the writer, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord. A person may plan his course, he adds, but it is the Lord who directs his steps, and he urges his readers to commit their work to him. The saying joins two truths that rarely sit easily together, that we are responsible for our plans and that we are not in control of the outcome.

Better is a little with righteousness, says the proverb, than great income with injustice. Better, it adds, is a dry crust eaten in peace than a house full of feasting with quarrelling. The sayings gently question the common idea that the richest life is the best, and they put a calm home above a full table.

A friend loves at all times, says the book, and a brother is born for adversity. It adds that some companions bring one another to ruin, while there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. Friendship, in these sayings, is tested most clearly in hard times, when loyalty costs something.

To answer before listening, the book says, is folly and shame, and the habit seems to be as old as speech itself. It is a simple rule, yet it is broken every day, because most of us are already preparing our reply while the other person is still talking. A great deal of misunderstanding might be avoided if we first heard the whole story.

Death and life are in the power of the tongue, says the writer, and those who love to talk will eat its fruit. The sentence reminds the reader that speech is never merely sound, because a kind word can heal and a cruel one can wound for years. What we say, the proverb teaches, matters as much as what we do, and sometimes a great deal more.

Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, says the book, and he will repay him for his deed. To oppress the poor, it adds, is to insult their Maker, while to be generous to them is to honour him. The proverb treats a person's treatment of the weak as a clear measure of his character.

Many are the plans in a person's mind, says the writer, but it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand. The saying does not forbid planning, for other proverbs praise careful thought, but it reminds the planner that the future is not in his hands. It encourages a mixture of effort and humility that many readers have found a comfort.

A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, says the book, and favour is better than silver or gold. Money, once lost, can be earned again, but a reputation for honesty, once spoiled, is far harder to rebuild. The saying invites the reader to think of character as the one possession that cannot be stolen but that can be thrown away.

Train up a child in the way he should go, says the writer, and even when he is old he will not depart from it. Parents have long found hope in this saying, although it describes a general pattern and not a guarantee for every child. It is a reminder that the habits we learn when young often follow us for a lifetime.

A section known as the Sayings of the Wise begins in the twenty-second chapter, and it contains advice on money, friendship and self-control. Do not wear yourself out to get rich, one saying says, and have the wisdom to stop, for riches can vanish in an instant, as though they had grown wings like an eagle and flown away. The warning is not against honest work but against a restless hunger for wealth that leaves no room for peace.

In the twenty-fifth chapter, the book says that the men of King Hezekiah copied out further proverbs of Solomon, and so we are told something about how the collection was put together. If your enemy is hungry, one of them says, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. In doing so, it adds, you will heap burning coals on his head, a puzzling picture that is often read as a way of shaming a person into goodness.

One verse tells the reader not to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be just like him. The very next verse says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes. The two sayings seem to contradict one another, and most readers conclude that judgment is needed to know which of them fits the moment.

As iron sharpens iron, says the book, so one person sharpens another, and a good friend is a whetstone for the mind. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, the writer adds, though the kisses of an enemy may be many, which suggests that honest criticism is a form of love. A true friend, in this view, is someone who makes us better and not merely someone who makes us comfortable.

A man named Agur, who speaks in the thirtieth chapter, offers a short prayer of rare honesty, asking God to give him neither poverty nor riches but only the food that he needs. He fears that if he is full, he may deny God, and that if he is poor, he may steal. He also confesses that four things are too wonderful for him, including an eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock and a ship at sea.

The book ends with a long poem about a capable woman, who rises early, works with her hands, manages her household with skill and opens her hand to the poor. She is clothed with strength and dignity, the poem says, and she speaks with wisdom, and her children rise up and call her blessed. Charm is deceptive and beauty fleeting, it concludes, but a woman who respects the Lord is to be praised, and so the book ends as it began, with wisdom lived out in the ordinary work of every day.
